items.excerpt: Building fire kills 14 in China's northern city of Taiyuan A fire on Sunday at a high-rise building in Taiyuan, the capital of China's northern province of Shanxi, killed at least 14 people, the official Xinhua news agency said on Monday. State media said 25 people were still in hospital, nine with serious injuries, citing authorities after the fire broke out on Sunday evening in the ​building on a busy downtown main road. Analysis-South African voters rebuff ANC, accelerating shift to coalition politics South Africans' sweeping rebuke of the African National Congress in local elections was a vote for performance over loyalty, analysts said, marking a political shift in which the former liberation movement can no ​longer call the shots. The ANC, widely criticised for corruption scandals and failing to deliver core public services, won less than a third of votes in the November 4 poll. It was ‌by far the worst result ​in history for the party that led the country out of apartheid under Nelson Mandela three decades ago. Lights go out at Russia's Novaya Gazeta, after years of defiant reporting Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta wound up its operations on Monday and quit its central Moscow office, bowing to what it said was a campaign of state pressure that had made it impossible to carry on reporting. Its co-founder Dmitry Muratov, addressing journalists who gathered to witness the newspaper's closure, issued an impassioned plea for free speech and human rights in wartime Russia. Greece retrieves bodies of 13 migrants in boat found off Crete, coast guard says Greece retrieved the bodies of 13 migrants along with 18 survivors from a boat that had been spotted by a container ship off the island of Crete early on Monday, its coast guard said. The Morocco-flagged container ship spotted the boat about 15 nautical miles (28 km) off the port of Kaloi Limenes on Crete. The coast guard said it had ‌taken the survivors and the dead to shore and that one of four people taken to hospital had later died there. Climate talks should focus on implementation, not new targets, Singapore says Global climate talks starting on Monday are unlikely to yield new targets on curbing greenhouse gases, but negotiators have plenty to do to implement measures already agreed, Singapore's environment minister said. "I think that we are not expecting a major upgrade in mitigation targets" at the annual UN talks in Turkey, Grace Fu told reporters. "But we have enough, even within the Paris Agreement, with what we have already agreed on. There is enough to work on." Nvidia probes whether CEO Huang was target of foreign spying as he admits affair Nvidia said on Sunday its board was probing whether CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, after a media report alleged he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Huang said in a message to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife and took "full responsibility" for his actions, while Nvidia said the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company without interruption. Steel plant blast kills 3, leaves 10 missing in western Turkey A blast at a steel and iron manufacturing plant in western Turkey on Monday killed 3 people and left 10 missing and 14 others were injured, the ‌local governor's office said. An explosion occurred at around noon (0900 GMT) at the Habas iron and steel manufacturing plant in the Aliaga district of the coastal Izmir province, the governor's office said in a statement Trump to meet Iran war mediator Qatar, no imminent deal seen to end the war US President Donald Trump will meet the prime minister of key mediator Qatar on Monday as efforts to end the Iran war ramp up following last week's midterm elections, though senior US and Gulf officials cast doubt on the chances of an imminent deal. With no victory in sight more than eight months into the conflict ‌he launched alongside Israel on February 28, Trump has played down the likelihood of major warfare restarting soon, but remains unwilling to accept an existing Iranian truce plan.

items.title: A key report for where inflation stood in October comes out Tuesday. Here's what to expect
items.excerpt: Published Mon, Nov 9 2026 4:03 PM EST ... - The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release the October consumer price index report Tuesday, with estimates of a 0.3% headline growth rate and 0.2% for core. - While the report won't include an annual rate because of last year's government shutdown, the results likely will keep the Fed well above its 2% inflation goal. ... Falling gasoline prices provided some relief to consumers in October, but Federal Reserve officials are increasingly concerned that inflation pressures elsewhere in the economy are proving harder to contain. Prices at the pump declined by more than 4%, according to the Energy Information Administration, providing a respite from a surge that had added more than a dollar a gallon over the past year. However, the consumer price index for the month, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics will release Tuesday at 8:30 a.m., is expected to show only a slight let-up. Meanwhile, Fed officials say they are worried that inflation initially driven higher by President Donald Trump's tariffs and the Iran war is proving more persistent than expected, with price pressures emerging in sectors beyond those directly affected by the shocks. At a time when the central bank is increasingly confident about the state of the labor market, concerns over the cost of living are what are top of mind for the Fed. "We've been moving up to what historically we'd consider full employment, and the big problem has all been on the inflation side. We go around, we talk to people everywhere in this district, all we hear about is affordability on the business side, the cost," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Monday during an event in his home district. "So we've got to come to terms with this cost-side and inflation-side failure." The CPI reading for all items is expected to show an increase of 0.3%. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, is forecast to increase 0.2%, according to the Dow Jones consensus forecast. While both would be slower than the respective September monthly gains of 0.6% and 0.3%, they still represent further price pressures. There will be no annual reading for October because of the government shutdown a year ago, which prevented the BLS from collecting some data and compiling a full index level. Because of the data issue, there isn't a comparable figure for the index. Bank of America, using an assumed baseline interpolating data for the period last year, estimated the annual growth rates at 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core, both 0.1 percentage point higher than September and well above the Fed's 2% goal. Goolsbee said the current run on inflation is defying what normally could be expected from supply shocks and tariffs, with the current situation intensified by the hyperscaler build-out related to artificial intelligence. "It was supposed to have gone away by now, and we're now starting to see the inflation kicking up in areas that probably weren't from oil prices and tariffs, like a bunch of services. Now this stuff with the AI data center build-out is, to my eyes, starting to look more just like old-fashioned demand overheating," he said. The massive investment in data centers is creating demand for construction workers, electricity and equipment, potentially adding to price pressures even as AI promises longer-term productivity gains, he added. ## Pressure on rates Though the Fed in October voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in place, markets are pricing in a better than 80% probability that the central bank will raise rates by a quarter percentage point at its next meeting in December, according to CME FedWatch data. Goolsbee, who doesn't vote on the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year but will in 2027, didn't commit to which way he was leaning on additional rate hikes, though he said current conditions could warrant action. "The conventional wisdom there is: Be aggressive up front, to never let the economy overheat, because once it gets overheated, it's extremely painful to get rid of that kind of overheating," he said. "So I think we've got to watch out in that space." The CPI release comes with economic growth strong — 3.4% in the third quarter for gross domestic product and tracking at 3.5% for the final three months of the year, according to the Atlanta Fed — and the labor market seemingly in solid shape as well. Nonfarm payrolls expanded by a much better-than-expected 165,000 in October, while the unemployment rate edged lower to 4.1%, though inflation-adjusted wage growth has been negative. That puts the inflation reading squarely in focus. Bank of America said it sees tariff impacts fading but that goods prices could be pushed higher because of AI demand. Further, the firm is cautious about "sticky" services prices as well as pressures from health insurance and autos. The bank has been hawkish in terms of Fed expectations and sees a December hike as likely so long as there isn't an escalated stock market sell-off that might dissuade the central bank. "This will be the final inflation report before the Fed's December 8-9 meeting. If our forecast is correct, we think it would effectively lock in another 25bp hike, all else equal," BofA economist Stephen Juneau said in a client note. "Absent an indisputably soft 0.1% [month-over-month] print, we doubt the inflation data will dissuade the Fed from hiking in December. The bigger risk to our call comes from financial markets."

items.title: Fed should move policy ’with care’ as it responds to inflation, Barkin says By Reuters
items.excerpt: GREER, South Carolina, Nov 9 (Reuters) - The US central bank should move its monetary policy "with care" as it maps a response to inflation that remains its greatest risk, Richmond Federal Reserve President Tom Barkin said on Monday, adding he had no base case for what should be done at the coming December meeting. "I don’t have a base case...We’ll get inflation. We’ll get another jobs report...Let’s see where the economy goes," Barkin told journalists after a local chamber of commerce event. "I am not going to predict...We are going to get to the meeting and figure it out." ... AI investment is a main prop of US economic growth right now but is also considered by many central bank policymakers as adding to inflation that remains well above the Fed’s 2% target. Investors currently expect the Fed to raise rates at the December 8-9 meeting as a way to put more downward pressure on the pace of price increases. As it stands, Barkin said in remarks to the Greater Greer Chamber of Commerce in South Carolina, businesses continue to face rising costs and say they are planning to try to pass them along. After nearly six years in which inflation has been above the Fed’s 2% target, "the risk lies on the inflation side of our dual mandate," Barkin said. "With demand healthy and inflation stubbornly elevated, the appropriate direction of monetary policy is relatively straightforward," said Barkin, who will become a voting member of the central bank’s policy-setting committee in 2027. But "it is wise to move policy with care," Barkin said, given risks that could hit the labor market and the Fed’s maximum employment goal.

items.title: BLS will omit 12-month CPI, Core CPI figures from October report By Investing.com
items.excerpt: Investing.com -- The Bureau of Labor Statistics will release its consumer price index report for October on Tuesday without the standard 12-month percentage change figures. The missing data stems from the 2025 government shutdown, which prevented BLS from collecting portions of price data for October 2025. The agency was unable to obtain that information retroactively, according to BLS spokesperson Cody Parkinson. The CPI report typically shows price changes compared to both the previous month and the prior year. The 12-month figure, which was 3.7% in September, is generally how the public understands inflation. Without the October 2025 data, BLS cannot calculate the 12-month percentage change for either the overall CPI or the core measure that excludes food and energy prices.

items.title: U.S. consumer prices seen rising 3.8% year-on-year in October - Truflation By Investing.com
items.excerpt: Investing.com - U.S. consumer prices are estimated to have risen by 3.8% in the twelve months to October and 0.3% month-on-month, amid ongoing upward pressure from elevated energy costs caused by the Iran war, according to Truflation predictions. ... Stripping out volatile items like food and fuel, the so-called "core" gauge is seen standing at 2.8% year-on-year and 0.2% month-on-month, the alternative data provider said in a statement. "Headline inflation is moderating, but upstream inflation pipeline remains active. Energy and tariffs are supporting renewed goods inflation. The key risk heading into 2027 is whether rising supply costs spread into persistent core inflation before consumer price sensitivity and moderating labor costs can offset them," Truflation said. The group added that it expects "uneven inflation" through the end of the year and early into 2027, with heightened goods prices due to tariffs and input expenses partially offset by stable services costs. Levies are seen pushing retail prices higher, although grocery prices are anticipated to fall because of retailer discounting and improving supplies. Energy is still the "principal swing factor" for overall price gains, Truflation flagged. For October, the group projected a 20.7% rise in energy prices versus a year earlier, with gasoline in particular climbing 37.7%. Month-on-month, gas price growth is tipped to moderate to 0.3%.

items.excerpt: ## What's ahead for lame-duck Congress session Congress returns today after a blue tsunami in the midterms swept Democrats into control of both chambers. But first, they have a lame-duck session to get through with Republicans still in charge — and a tall list of tasks to complete. Here are some of the top items: → Fund the government: Lawmakers have to avert a shutdown on Dec. 11. Many were hoping to approve a full-year appropriations bill, but that’s far from certain as Iran war funding emerges as a flash point. → House leadership races: House Republicans will choose their leadership team tomorrow in a secret-ballot election. Speaker Mike Johnson’s departure sets up a race for minority leader between Reps. Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan.

items.title: Trump administration live updates: Congress returns with government funding atop the to-do list
items.excerpt: November 09, 2026, 7:50 PM EST By NBC News ## What to know today - CONGRESS IS BACK: Congress returns today for a lame-duck session after Democrats delivered a crushing defeat to Republicans in the midterm elections. The first order of business on the tall list of tasks is funding the government to avert a shutdown in December. - HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT EFFORT: Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., reintroduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the U.S. war with Iran and other military actions ordered by President Donald Trump. - SENATE LEADERSHIP: A growing number of Republican senators are calling for a delay in their leadership elections tomorrow morning to discuss contenders' plans after the GOP's midterm losses. - UNCALLED RACES: Vote counting continues in the Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi, where Democratic candidates Mary Peltola and Scott Colom narrowly lead their respective Republican opponents, Sens. Dan Sullivan and Cindy Hyde-Smith. ... ## Trump casts doubt on election results after saying he was ‘absolutely willing’ to accept them Days after he said he was “ absolutely willing” to accept the massive Republican losses in the midterm elections, Trump suggested today on social media that the Democratic victories weren’t “honest.” “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting ‘dumps’ were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote,” he wrote on Truth Social, implying there was something nefarious about elections carried out under different processes in different states. “It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!” the post concluded, without elaborating. Election officials nationwide have reported that voting this year was largely routine. Asked about the post, a White House official noted that Trump had told reporters ahead of last week’s elections that he would respect the results “if they’re honest elections.” ... ## Rep. Thomas Massie unveils impeachment articles against Hegseth Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., today unveiled articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. If Massie introduces the impeachment articles as privileged, he will force a House floor vote by Wednesday. Massie says he will bring eight charges, including three charges related to allegations that Hegseth violated sections of the War Powers Resolution of 1973. The first article "charges Secretary Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat," Massie's press release said. "It establishes that the war was unlawful from its inception." Rep. Thomas Massie. Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty Article 1 of the Constitution says that Congress has the power to declare war. The last time Congress formally declared war, though, was World War II. The War Powers Resolution says that any time the military is used and war hasn't been declared, the president has to formally notify the House Speaker and Senate president pro tempore within two days. The president must also end the use of armed forces within 60 days if the president uses the military without prior notification to Congress, according to the resolution. The articles of impeachment that Massie introduced also include charges related to alleged "extrajudicial killings," referring to the strikes on alleged drug boats; "kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader," referring to the U.S. capturing now-former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro; and "unlawful war in Yemen." "My effort to impeach Secretary Hegseth is a much gentler version of what’s coming when the Democrats assume control of the House and Senate next year," Massie said in a statement. "They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate." Hegseth plans to hold a press conference tomorrow morning to address the impeachment efforts.

items.excerpt: ### Godzilla Minus Zero’s record opening, Ramayana’s ₹500 crore Diwali weekend, a strong start for Wild Horse Nine & I Play Rocky, and a Bond announcement due. ... The weekend box office, worldwide: Godzilla Minus Zero topped the worldwide chart with an estimated $63 million, made up of a record-setting $31.6 million from 3,254 cinemas in North America, plus about $17 million in Japan over the weekend, and the rest from other markets. It’s the biggest-ever North American opening for a live-action foreign-language film, beating the $17.8 million of China’s Hero in 2002, and IMAX generated $21.3 million globally, or 34% of the takings. India’s Ramayana: Rise of a Legend, as it’s known abroad, was second worldwide with about $52 million, according to Screen’s figures, although Deadline has it at $55 million. Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine opened to $6 million in North America from 1,100 cinemas, in eighth place, and $6.6 million from 29 other markets, a $12.6 million worldwide start. Warner Bros.’ The Cat in the Hat was second in North America with $20.5 million, plus another $10 million internationally, which is a disappointment against a $92 million budget, although audiences gave it an ‘A’ CinemaScore. Elsewhere, Amazon MGM’s I Play Rocky opened in just seven cinemas in North America, taking $345,000 for a strong $49,200 per-cinema average, and You Can See Everything fell just 23% in its fourth weekend to $8.8 million, taking it to $79.8 million in North America. These are Sunday studio estimates, with the confirmed numbers due later today. ... Ramayana’s Diwali weekend: Nitesh Tiwari’s Ramayana: Part 1 passed a worldwide gross of ₹499.20 crore (about $52 million) after four days, according to Sacnilk, and it’s now just short of ₹500 crore. After a 26% drop on Friday, it bounced back 45% on Saturday, with ₹69.80 crore net in India (about $7.3 million), followed by ₹56.15 crore (about $5.8 million) on Diwali Sunday. That took its India net total to ₹238.85 crore (about $25 million), but narrowly missed the all-time top ten opening weekends in India. It opens in Hong Kong on Thursday, and I’ll bring you the full numbers once the figures settle.
